newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Horsham, Trizec propose merger.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Horsham, Trizec propose merger.

text.p: (All figures in U.S. dollars unless otherwise specified)

Canadian resource and real estate holding company Horsham Corp. said on Tuesday it proposed a merger with Trizec Corp. Ltd., in which it holds a 48 percent stake, in a deal that would create a real estate company with a market capitalisation topping $1.5 billion.
Toronto-based Trizec is one of North America's largest publicly traded real estate firms.
Besides its holdings in Trizec, Horsham also has stakes in Toronto-based Barrick Gold Corp., the world's third biggest gold producer, and St. Louis-based refiner Clark USA Inc.
But this deal would transform it fully into a real estate operating company.

The merged entity would be called Trizec Hahn Corp. -- after Trizec and its U.S. shopping centre unit, the Hahn Co. Under the proposal, Trizec shareholders other than Horsham would receive 0.58 of a subordinated voting share of Trizec Hahn for each Trizec common share.

Executives said the company will help Horsham shake off its "conglomerate discount" -- a term investment professionals use to explain the fact that shares in holding companies are often valued lower by the market than their components.
"The discount to its net asset value has widened over time rather than shrunk," said president Greg Wilkins at a news briefing.
Trizec has been fighting its way back from insolvency since 1994. Horsham has provided it with capital but it still needs more to catapult it back into the top ranks of real estate acquisitors.

"Horsham on the other side is rich with capital and the marriage of its capital with Trizec's asset base and its management expertise...makes the vehicle more attractive to institutional shareholders," Wilkins said.
Subject to the approval of Trizec Hahn's board, Horsham also proposed that the merged entity raise dividends with an initial increase to 25 cents a share.

Horsham Chairman Peter Munk would be chairman and chief executive of Trizec Hahn, while Greg Wilkins, president of both Horsham and Trizec, would become president and chief operating officer of the merged entity.

Munk, one of Canada's better-known businessmen, plans to take Trizec Hahn onto the global stage, building shopping malls in such places of growing demand as Central Europe, Southeast Asia and Latin America.

"I think retailers, whether it's Disney...or the new restaurant owners, or The Gap, and The Limited, or all those people are looking for international expansion. They want operators of shopping malls with whom they have had experience for years or decades," Munk said.

Trizec established a special committee of the board of directors to consider the Horsham proposal. The deal is subject to the approval of regulators and the holders of a majority of Trizec's common shares other than Horsham.
The proposal was based on arm's length talks with Argo Partnership L.P., Trizec's 26 percent shareholder.

Separately, Trizec said the merged entity would "continue the process of realising on the value of Clark in the near term and optimizing the benefit of the Barrick holding." The Barrick shares are worth more than $800 million on the open market, Trizec said.
Wilkins told reporters Horsham is in talks with a number of possible buyers for its 46 percent-held Clark USA Inc. unit and hopes to unveil a deal before the end of the year.
Trizec was up C75 cents to a new 52-week high of C$11.25 ($8.21), and Horsham rose C70 cents to C$18.95 ($13.83) in afternoon trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
